system: Jadera haematoloma (soapberry bug) diverged after colonizing new Asian host in Florida
coordinate_notes: https://tools.wmflabs.org/geohack/geohack.php?pagename=Key_Largo&params=25.0865_N_-80.4473_E_type:isle_region:US-FL_source:OSM. locality, a foew other sites available
gtime_notes: From the paper (Carrol 1997): Generation time is about 40 d (measured in captivity at 30 ºC). There is a large difference between the host species in the annual pattern of seed availability. In the introduced host, a much larger seed crop is available for a much briefer annual period, while in the native host, smaller seed crops are available year-round. There is time for two or three generations of bugs to develop on the introduced host, while more generations may develop in the Keys on the native host depending on how individual bugs move among sequential seed crops on different host individuals. We take the generation time on the new host (gorne 2022).
who: Hendry et al 2007; Erika included this recored in her 'correction spreadsheet'.

gtime_notes: From the paper (Carrol 1997): Generation time is about 40 d (measured in captivity at 30 ºC). There is a large difference between the host species in the annual pattern of seed availability. In the introduced host, a much larger seed crop is available for a much briefer annual period, while in the native host, smaller seed crops are available year-round. There is time for two or three generations of bugs to develop on the introduced host, while more generations may develop in the Keys on the native host depending on how individual bugs move among sequential seed crops on different host individuals. We take the generation time on the new host (gorne 2022).

system: Poecilia reticulata (Trinidadian guppy) populations respond to different predation regimes following introductions in Trinidad from high predation to low predation
sample2: Derived pop introduced in low predation stream (X)
coordinate_notes: From Gotanda et al. 2013 Oecologia
gtime_notes: from Reznick 1997: "Guppies breed throughout the year and have overlapping generations. We estimated generation time T using the life table method, which is based on estimates of birth and death schedules in natural populations. We estimated mortality rates from mark-recapture experiments on guppies from seven low-predation localities, including the Aripo and El Cedro experimental sites. Because the life table method requires age-specific survival, we estimated the ages of individuals in different size classes using growth rate equations derived for the same fish in the mark-recapture experiments based on their sizes at the beginning and end of the recapture interval. We estimated size-specific fecundity with dissections and embryo counts from females collected from these same localities, plus from additional collections. We estimated the frequency of reproduction from laboratory studies, conducted at temperatures and food availabilities similar to those in the field. With this information, we estimated the mean generation time of fish in low-predation localities to be 210 days, or 1.74 generations per year". So, gtime=0.575.
comments: Values were re-extracted following Hendry and Kinnison 1999: "Rates were calculated using nleans and standard errors estimated from figure 4 in Endler (1980). Sample sizes were 100 (J. Endler, pers. cotnm.). The genetic basis for divergence was not explicitly nleasured, but male guppy color patterns have a genetic basis. Endler (1980) estimated that 15 generations had passed (about 8.3 generations/yr), but a life-table analysis by Reznick et al. (1997) indicated that guppies in the Aripo River have 1.74 generations per year. We used Reznick's value."

system: Branta leucopsis (Barnacle Goose) body size decline in Sweden
comments_on_system: Kjell Larsson kindly provided the dataset with means, SDs, and Ns. The dataset has time series for tarsus and head length by sex, colony (two colonies), and two grouping types. From the two grouping types, we chose to compare only temporally extreme samples for breeding/captured populations (i.e. not use the cohort grouping). Although these birds are long lived (> 15 y), because samples are spaced by about ten years, it is likely that onlt a few birds were included in both allochronic samples.
comments: Old rates based on regressions. Current means, SDs and Ns, based on extreme samples in the time series using the data sent by the author.
reference_comments: Kjell Larsson kindly provided means, SD, and N, for each year, colony, and trait
who: Hendry et al 2007 included rates based on regression lines. Now, rates are based on extreme samples for the time series using data obtained from the author (CC).

system: Poecilia reticulata (Trinidadian guppy) populations respond to different predation regimes following introductions in Trinidad from high predation to low predation
coordinate_notes: From Gotanda et al. 2013 Oecologia
gtime_notes: from Reznick 1997: "Guppies breed throughout the year and have overlapping generations. We estimated generation time T using the life table method, which is based on estimates of birth and death schedules in natural populations. We estimated mortality rates from mark-recapture experiments on guppies from seven low-predation localities, including the Aripo and El Cedro experimental sites. Because the life table method requires age-specific survival, we estimated the ages of individuals in different size classes using growth rate equations derived for the same fish in the mark-recapture experiments based on their sizes at the beginning and end of the recapture interval. We estimated size-specific fecundity with dissections and embryo counts from females collected from these same localities, plus from additional collections. We estimated the frequency of reproduction from laboratory studies, conducted at temperatures and food availabilities similar to those in the field. With this information, we estimated the mean generation time of fish in low-predation localities to be 210 days, or 1.74 generations per year". So, gtime=0.575.
trait_description: schooling tendency (number of s in 5 min trials)
reference: Magurran 1992, Proc. R. Soc. Lond. B 248: 117-122
who: Hendry et al 2007; Andrew added the original data.

system: Poecilia reticulata (Trinidadian guppy) populations respond to different predation regimes following introductions in Trinidad from high predation to low predation
coordinate_notes: From Gotanda et al. 2013 Oecologia
gtime_notes: from Reznick 1997: "Guppies breed throughout the year and have overlapping generations. We estimated generation time T using the life table method, which is based on estimates of birth and death schedules in natural populations. We estimated mortality rates from mark-recapture experiments on guppies from seven low-predation localities, including the Aripo and El Cedro experimental sites. Because the life table method requires age-specific survival, we estimated the ages of individuals in different size classes using growth rate equations derived for the same fish in the mark-recapture experiments based on their sizes at the beginning and end of the recapture interval. We estimated size-specific fecundity with dissections and embryo counts from females collected from these same localities, plus from additional collections. We estimated the frequency of reproduction from laboratory studies, conducted at temperatures and food availabilities similar to those in the field. With this information, we estimated the mean generation time of fish in low-predation localities to be 210 days, or 1.74 generations per year". So, gtime=0.575.

system: Gambusia affinis (mosquitofish) diversify on Hawaiian islands sites after introduction of single stock
comments_on_system: Many reservoirs;.all paiwise comparisons and selected traits included (CC). This study documents the degree to which six populations of mosquitofish that shared common ancestors in 1905 had diverged by 1980. Note that since the old database, the number of years indexed is 70 rather than 75 (1980-1905). SD were obtained from CI and t-distribution with alpha = 0,05, and df = N-1. The SDs in the old database were obtained the same way, but using N in stead of df. In the paper there's no indication if a t or normal distribution was used to calcualte the CIs, but Stearns was mentioned in the acknowledgements of Hendy and Kinnison 1999 (CC).

system: Passerella iliaca (fox sparrow) temporal variation in California
comments_on_system: This system involve seven populations in California, some considered subspecies. For each population, data for allochronic rates were included herein. Ten variables with high measurement error (sensu Zink 1983) were excluded. Re-measured samples were also excluded. For the recent samples, the year with higher sample size was used (two sites had data for three years).
coordinate_notes: From Google Maps.
reference_comments: Full dataset for males was provided by the author. Following Zink (1983), ten characters were excluded from the database due to relatively high levels of measurement error (CC).
who: Hendry et al 2007 included percent change data provided in the paper (populations pooled). These records were excluded, and data provided by the author was included (CC).

time_series: No, but data can be put together from different years.

who: Hendry et al 2007 included rates comparing populations from the extreme of the distribution range. Now, all parwise comparissons were included using a new dataset provided by the author (April 2010, CC).

system: Gasterosteus aculeatus (Threespine stickleback) naturally colonizing Logberg Lake Alaska (1982)
comments_on_system: s070, s307 and s309 are similar but different populations

comments: Haldanes & darwins are also given in the ms

system: Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito) expands its range and diversify after introduction into the USA from temperate Asia
comments_on_system: Moore 1999 describes the system and cronology detailed. The sequence of colonization is TX -> FL -> NJ
coordinate_notes: Estimated from Google Maps based on Figure in Manuscript. region� one landmark to represent many sites in New Jersey, Florida and Texas (latitudes given)
gtime_notes: According to Nur Aida et al 2008 (Trop Biomed 25(2): 117-125), the generation time is 20.14 days (0.055 years), but this is in the lab. It does not take into account the winter in USA. According Waldock et al 2013 (Pathogens and Global Health 107(5): 224-241) in North America, a photoperiod of 13:11 (L:D) induces diapause in Ae. albopictus. I (gorne) computed the number generations in one year according to the number of days longer than 13 hours in one year. Then computed the generation time as the average of the gtime (reciprocal of the number of generations in one year) in both locations. i.e. Florida 5.38 G/y (113 days), Texas 5.81 G/y (122 days), New York 6.95 G/y (146 days).
reference: Armbruster and Conn 2006, Annals of the Entomological Society of America 99(6): 1234-1243

coordinate_notes: Estimated from Google Maps based on Figure in Manuscript. region� one landmark to represent many sites in New Jersey, Florida and Texas (latitudes given)
gtime_notes: According to Nur Aida et al 2008 (Trop Biomed 25(2): 117-125), the generation time is 20.14 days (0.055 years), but this is in the lab. It does not take into account the winter in USA. According Waldock et al 2013 (Pathogens and Global Health 107(5): 224-241) in North America, a photoperiod of 13:11 (L:D) induces diapause in Ae. albopictus. I (gorne) computed the number generations in one year according to the number of days longer than 13 hours in one year. Then computed the generation time as the average of the gtime (reciprocal of the number of generations in one year) in both locations. i.e. Florida 5.38 G/y (113 days), Texas 5.81 G/y (122 days), New York 6.95 G/y (146 days).
trait_description: developmental period (number of days from larval hatch to pupation)
reference: Armbruster and Conn 2006, Annals of the Entomological Society of America 99(6): 1234-1243

gtime_notes: According to Nur Aida et al 2008 (Trop Biomed 25(2): 117-125), the generation time is 20.14 days (0.055 years), but this is in the lab. It does not take into account the winter in USA. coordinate_notes: Estimated from Google Maps based on Figure in Manuscript. region� one landmark to represent many sites in New Jersey, Florida and Texas (latitudes given)
gtime_notes: According to Nur Aida et al 2008 (Trop Biomed 25(2): 117-125), the generation time is 20.14 days (0.055 years), but this is in the lab. It does not take into account the winter in USA. According Waldock et al 2013 (Pathogens and Global Health 107(5): 224-241) in North America, a photoperiod of 13:11 (L:D) induces diapause in Ae. albopictus. I (gorne) computed the number generations in one year according to the number of days longer than 13 hours in one year. Then computed the generation time as the average of the gtime (reciprocal of the number of generations in one year) in both locations. i.e. Florida 5.38 G/y (113 days), Texas 5.81 G/y (122 days), New York 6.95 G/y (146 days).
trait_description: growth rate (pupal mass divided by preadult developmental period)
reference: Armbruster and Conn 2006, Annals of the Entomological Society of America 99(6): 1234-1243

system: Onthophagus taurus (dung beetle) diverged between introduced pops. of USA and Australia, derived from putatively similar Mediterranean ancestor
coordinate_notes: Wikipedia and Google Maps. locality
gtime_notes: Under good conditions Onthophagus taurus display 2 generations each year (https://www.ukbeetles.co.uk/onthophagus-taurus). The adults are active from early spring to late autumn, they pair up in the spring. The development is rapid and under optimum conditions of nutrition and temperature the cycle from egg to adult takes eight to ten weeks, there are often two generations each year and in warmer climates this is the norm. Well fed and later instar larvae will overwinter in the brood chamber, continuing to feed in mild spells and producing very early spring adults. Those that eclose and emerge in the autumn will return to the burrow to overwinter.
reference: Moczek et al. 2002, Evolutionary Ecology Research 4: 587-601

system: Gadus morhua (Atlantic cod) subjected to fishing pressure in Newfoundland and Labrador
coordinate_notes: From http://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=details&id=23382.. open sea
trait_description: Length at 50% maturation probability at a given age (cm)
comments: Rates given in paper, but they were recalculated using sample moments sent by the author; all possible rates using the extreme of the time series for each stock, sex, and age class (5 or 6) were calculated. Values in the SDs columns correspond to the SEs assuming normality; were calculated from bootstrap confidence intervals provided by the author, and they are not appropriate to calculate Haldanes (CC). Sample sizes are available in the study's folder; were sent by the author in a later date to AM, but are not necessary to calculate Darwins (CC). Kiyoko added sample sizes.
reference_comments: The author kindly provided sample's moments.
who: Ann got the sample moments from the author; CC selected and indexed data into the DB.

coordinate_notes: averages calculated from lat in paper and longs provided by author when possible (longs: Australia, Chile, and Europe). Remaining longs found with Google Maps. region
gtime_notes: Ulex europaeus starts to reproduce at 2 or 3 years old. It lives up to 30 years old. It follows the −3/2 law of self-thinning (Rees M & Hill RL. 2001. Large-scale disturbances, biological control and the dynamics of gorse populations. J Appl Ecol 38:364–377). We assume that an increase in fecundity with age compensates for mortality, so the contribution of each age to the next generation is constant. This assumption probably underestimates the generation time, but less than just using the age at maturity.
comments: Kiyoko - I am including range expansion in this reference (and systems) even though the article does not explicitly state range expansion because the invasives have such widespread ranges that they clearly expanded after introduction

system: Lythrum salicaria (purple loosestrife) introduced into North America diverged from native European plants
coordinate_notes: From http://dateandtime.info/citycoordinates.php?id=5122432 and wikipedia. Coordinates of one site entered; two other sites in USA available (Chun 2007); locality (Blossey ref. ) but not plotted as the site in Chun 2007 was used to represent the system.
gtime_notes: "The species has been described as a facultative annual because it can set seed in one growing season (Shipley and Parent 1991, Johansson and Keddy 1991), however, this description is misleading because the species is not semelparous. Lythrum salicaria is a perennial, with annual stems arising from a perennating rootstock. There are no reports in the literature concerning the longevity of single genets." (Mal TR, Lovett-Doust J, Lovett-Doust L & Mulligan GA. 1992. The biology of Canadian weeds. 100. Lythrum salicaria. Canadian Journal of Plant Science, 72:1305-1330.). Generation time was computed from COMPADRE database transition matices (Matrices 244356, 244359 in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/46816 [21 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0])

coordinate_notes: from several populations, so averaged. region; one of several regions in three states plotted (two references).

system: Solidago gigantea (giant goldenrod) introduced to Europe from North America
coordinate_notes: Used coordinates from V008 ref_ID p085 s173 (Meyer 2005) because similar sampling ranges. one region out of three in western europe was plotted
gtime_notes: Solidago gigantea is very simmilar to Solidago altissima (see Solidago altissima GTimeNotes). Solidago gigantea is a tall, erect perennial herb with annual aboveground shoots and persistent belowground rhizomes. Solidago gigantea produces long-creeping plagiotropic, mostly purple or reddish rhizomes, mostly within the upper 10–20 cm of soil. In total, 3–50 rhizomes per ramet emerge close to the base of shoots from the previous year. Higher numbers have been observed after disturbances. Production of seeds, new shoots and new rhizomes occurs every year, and all aboveground shoots die back in autumn. Free carbohydrates are accumulated in the rhizome before the dormant period. Seedlings have never been observed within established patches of S. gigantea, suggesting that seeds are primarily important for long-distance dispersal and the colonization of new sites. However, seedlings may appear after a spring mowing, suggesting that successful establishment is dependent upon open conditions. In most cases, however, population increase is primarily the result of clonal growth. The relative significance of sexual reproduction increases with the age of the clone, whereas clonal growth is most essential during the first years after establishment. Individual clones are often easy to distinguish and frequently achieve 2–5 m diameter. Larger, older clones may contain thousands of ramets. Occasionally clones form ‘fairy circles’ around the initial centre of the genet. Under good conditions, almost all plants reproduce in their first year, and a single ramet produces up to 19,000 achenes. Under resource limited conditions, sexual reproduction is reduced to the benefit of vegetative growth (Weber E & Jakobs G. 2005. Biological flora of central Europe: Solidago gigantea Aiton. Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants, 200:109–118). Generation time should be long but I did not find any estimation. However, Meyer et al 2005 (Meyer G, Clare R, Weber E. 2005. An experimental test of the evolution of increased competitive ability hypothesis in goldenrod, Solidago gigantea. Oecologia, 144:299-307) observed that almost all plants grown from seeds flowered in the secon year, more than a half flowered in the first year. So, in newly colonized areas a generation time of 2 years can be assumed. This would be a far underestimation for established populations.

gtime_notes: Lactuca muralis a herbaceous perennial hemicryptophyte. The plant is winter green dying completely back after flowering in the summer but then producing a small overwintering rosette(s) from a bud(s) on the rootstock. The plant is generally not monocarpic. Reproduction is entirely by seed. Most seeds germinate in the autumn and overwinter as a small rosette although some germinate in the following spring. Newly shed achenes germinate readily, giving rise in nature to seedling populations immediately after the flowering period. Seeds may also germinate after overwintering in the following spring. gtime_notes: Senecio sylvaticus is an annual, mostly autogamous plant. S. sylvaticus is rooting in the litter layer (A00) and fermentation layer (A0) and is very unproductive on mineral soils. Achenes of S. sylvaticus genninated in Autum or in Spring. The biomass of the winter annual life forms was more than ten fold that of the summer annual life form in the last days of May. coordinate_notes: used means from lat long reported in Table 1 for species of interest. region, coordinates of several sites available
gtime_notes: Digitalis purpurea is a facultative biennial, a monocarpic species that can complete their life cycle within 2 years, but where a delay of reproduction until the third or later year is commonly observed because it must reach a threshold size to be able to be vernalized (Sletvold N. 2002. Effects of plant size on reproductive output and offspring performance in the facultative biennial Digitalis purpurea. Journal of Ecology, 90:958-966). While, 19% of seeds germinates in the same year their are release (in autum), 48% germinates in the following spring (Van Baalen J. 1982. Germination ecology and seed population dynamics of Digitalis purpurea. Oecologia, 53:61-67). Germination in autum allow a life cycle of one year, germination in springs allow a life cycle of two years (because vernalization is required). But also is posible that plants germinated in autum do not reach the size threshold required to be vernalized. Generation time computed from transitions matrices in COMPADRE database (Matrices 242803, 242806 in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/46874 [18 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0]) vary from 3.47 to 7.84 years

system: Echium vulgare (viper's bugloss or blueweed) introduced in Australia in common garden with native British and Europe plants
coordinate_notes: used means from lat long reported in Table 1 for species of interest. Region. Several lakes studied, coodinates available in paper.
gtime_notes: The plant species E. vulgare (vipers's bugloss) is a self-compatible monocarpic perennial. Plants flowered at a mean age of 2.7 years on the sparse site and 3.4 years on the dense sites (Klemow KM & Raynal DJ. 1985. Demography of Two Facultative Biennial Plant Species in an Unproductive Habitat. The Journal of Ecology, 73:147-167). Levels of innate seed dormancy vary among populations, germination without cold stratification is low (less than 20%). Seed dispersal begins in mid Summer and continues through mid Autum. Most seedlings emerge in the spring (Klemow KM, Clements DR, Threadgill PF & Cavers PB. 2002. The biology of Canadian weeds. 116. Echium vulgare L. Canadian journal of plant science, 82:235-248). So, generation time is 3.5 years (3 for flowering plus 6 month for stratification). The generation time computed from transition matrix in COMPADRE database (Matrix 242943 in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/46613 [18 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0]) is consistent, 3.67ys

system: Solidago gigantea (giant goldenrod) introduced to Europe from North America
coordinate_notes: Used coordinates from V008 ref_ID p085 s173 (Meyer 2005) because similar sampling ranges. one region out of three in western europe was plotted
gtime_notes: Solidago gigantea is very simmilar to Solidago altissima (see Solidago altissima GTimeNotes). Solidago gigantea is a tall, erect perennial herb with annual aboveground shoots and persistent belowground rhizomes. Solidago gigantea produces long-creeping plagiotropic, mostly purple or reddish rhizomes, mostly within the upper 10–20 cm of soil. In total, 3–50 rhizomes per ramet emerge close to the base of shoots from the previous year. Higher numbers have been observed after disturbances. Production of seeds, new shoots and new rhizomes occurs every year, and all aboveground shoots die back in autumn. Free carbohydrates are accumulated in the rhizome before the dormant period. Seedlings have never been observed within established patches of S. gigantea, suggesting that seeds are primarily important for long-distance dispersal and the colonization of new sites. However, seedlings may appear after a spring mowing, suggesting that successful establishment is dependent upon open conditions. In most cases, however, population increase is primarily the result of clonal growth. The relative significance of sexual reproduction increases with the age of the clone, whereas clonal growth is most essential during the first years after establishment. Individual clones are often easy to distinguish and frequently achieve 2–5 m diameter. Larger, older clones may contain thousands of ramets. Occasionally clones form ‘fairy circles’ around the initial centre of the genet. Under good conditions, almost all plants reproduce in their first year, and a single ramet produces up to 19,000 achenes. Under resource limited conditions, sexual reproduction is reduced to the benefit of vegetative growth (Weber E & Jakobs G. 2005. Biological flora of central Europe: Solidago gigantea Aiton. Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants, 200:109–118). Generation time should be long but I did not find any estimation. However, Meyer et al 2005 (Meyer G, Clare R, Weber E. 2005. An experimental test of the evolution of increased competitive ability hypothesis in goldenrod, Solidago gigantea. Oecologia, 144:299-307) observed that almost all plants grown from seeds flowered in the secon year, more than a half flowered in the first year. So, in newly colonized areas a generation time of 2 years can be assumed. This would be a far underestimation for established populations.

Solidago gigantea produces long-creeping plagiotropic, mostly purple or reddish rhizomes, mostly within the upper 10–20 cm of soil. In total, 3–50 rhizomes per ramet emerge close to the base of shoots from the previous year. Higher numbers have been observed after disturbances. Production of seeds, new shoots and new rhizomes occurs every year, and all aboveground shoots die back in autumn. Free carbohydrates are accumulated in the rhizome before the dormant period. Seedlings have never been observed within established patches of S. gigantea, suggesting that seeds are primarily important for long-distance dispersal and the colonization of new sites. However, seedlings may appear after a spring mowing, suggesting that successful establishment is dependent upon open conditions. In most cases, however, population increase is primarily the result of clonal growth. The relative significance of sexual reproduction increases with the age of the clone, whereas clonal growth is most essential during the first years after establishment. Individual clones are often easy to distinguish and frequently achieve 2–5 m diameter. Larger, older clones may contain thousands of ramets. Occasionally clones form ‘fairy circles’ around the initial centre of the genet. Under good conditions, almost all plants reproduce in their first year, and a single ramet produces up to 19,000 achenes. Under resource limited conditions, sexual reproduction is reduced to the benefit of vegetative growth (Weber E & Jakobs G. 2005. Biological flora of central Europe: Solidago gigantea Aiton. Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants, 200:109–118). Generation time should be long but I did not find any estimation. However, Meyer et al 2005 (Meyer G, Clare R, Weber E. 2005. An experimental test of the evolution of increased competitive ability hypothesis in goldenrod, Solidago gigantea. Oecologia, 144:299-307) observed that almost all plants grown from seeds flowered in the secon year, more than a half flowered in the first year. So, in newly colonized areas a generation time of 2 years can be assumed. This would be a far underestimation for established populations.

system: Cyprinodon tularosa (white sands pupfish) diverge between native creek pop and two intro pond pop in in the Tularosa Basin, southern New Mexico.
comments_on_system: I can tell you that generation time is pretty short in White Sands pupfish (1-2 generations per year) and related to population density. If introduced to a new environment, larval pupfish will mature within a few months. With a long breeding season (maybe 7-8 months), it means that theoretically 2 generations per year are possible. But, breeding is also hierarchical. Largest males obtain and defend breeding territories. Even males that mature might have to wait until they can obtain breeding territories. Thus, it might be safer with dense populations to estimate that generation time is one year. I'm not sure if this affects females though (maybe smaller, younger females are not restricted as much from breeding once mature). I typically reference a range of generations when discussing something like evolutionary divergence. For example, in reference to the introduced populations discussed in the 2005 Copeia paper, the time of introduction was approximately 30 years before the study so I guess 30-60 generations in the wild. If I were to calculate something like a Haldane, I would probably use 0.5 years (or 60 generations in 30 years) for generation time to be conservative. (M. Collier).

system: Poecilia reticulata (Trinidadian guppies) phenotypic variation in Marianne river, Trinidad
comments_on_system: Same system as 407 but different disturbance and different driver
gtime_notes: from Reznick 1997: "Guppies breed throughout the year and have overlapping generations. We estimated generation time T using the life table method, which is based on estimates of birth and death schedules in natural populations. We estimated mortality rates from mark-recapture experiments on guppies from seven low-predation localities, including the Aripo and El Cedro experimental sites. Because the life table method requires age-specific survival, we estimated the ages of individuals in different size classes using growth rate equations derived for the same fish in the mark-recapture experiments based on their sizes at the beginning and end of the recapture interval. We estimated size-specific fecundity with dissections and embryo counts from females collected from these same localities, plus from additional collections. We estimated the frequency of reproduction from laboratory studies, conducted at temperatures and food availabilities similar to those in the field. With this information, we estimated the mean generation time of fish in low-predation localities to be 210 days, or 1.74 generations per year". So, gtime=0.575.
reference_comments: Author provided data

We estimated mortality rates from mark-recapture experiments on guppies from seven low-predation localities, including the Aripo and El Cedro experimental sites. Because the life table method requires age-specific survival, we estimated the ages of individuals in different size classes using growth rate equations derived for the same fish in the mark-recapture experiments based on their sizes at the beginning and end of the recapture interval. We estimated size-specific fecundity with dissections and embryo counts from females collected from these same localities, plus from additional collections. We estimated the frequency of reproduction from laboratory studies, conducted at temperatures and food availabilities similar to those in the field. With this information, we estimated the mean generation time of fish in low-predation localities to be 210 days, or 1.74 generations per year". So, gtime=0.575.

Poecilia reticulata (Trinidadian guppies) from HP (Yarra) environment introduced to a LP and HP (Damier) habitats; measurements from eight years after introduction, Trinidad
coordinate_notes: Approximate coordinates based on map provided in article
gtime_notes: from Reznick 1997: "Guppies breed throughout the year and have overlapping generations. We estimated generation time T using the life table method, which is based on estimates of birth and death schedules in natural populations. We estimated mortality rates from mark-recapture experiments on guppies from seven low-predation localities, including the Aripo and El Cedro experimental sites. Because the life table method requires age-specific survival, we estimated the ages of individuals in different size classes using growth rate equations derived for the same fish in the mark-recapture experiments based on their sizes at the beginning and end of the recapture interval. We estimated size-specific fecundity with dissections and embryo counts from females collected from these same localities, plus from additional collections. We estimated the frequency of reproduction from laboratory studies, conducted at temperatures and food availabilities similar to those in the field. With this information, we estimated the mean generation time of fish in low-predation localities to be 210 days, or 1.74 generations per year". So, gtime=0.575.

gtime_notes: Senecio sylvaticus is an annual, mostly autogamous plant. Within the group of annual Senecio species, S. sylvaticus is not as strict summer annual as the co-occurring S. viscosus, but has also not such a variable seasonality as S. vulgaris. S. sylvaticus is rooting in the litter layer (A00) and fermentation layer (A0) and is very unproductive on mineral soils. Achenes of S. sylvaticus genninated in Autum or in Spring. From late Spring to mid Summer no germination was observed. In addition to the two different periods of gennination, there was a great difference in plant biomass of both life forms in spring. The biomass of the winter annual life forms was more than ten fold that of the summer annual life form in the last days of May. Under natural conditions, the summer annual populations did flower from summer to autum. (Ernst, W. H. O. (1989). Selection of winter and summer annual life forms in populations of Senecio sylvaticus L. Flora, 182(3-4), 221-231)

system: Lactuca muralis (wall lettuce) change dispersal potential after colonizing islands with respect to mainland (source) population in BC, Canada
coordinate_notes: laction names and map in paper. coordinates searched in googlemaps
gtime_notes: Lactuca muralis a herbaceous perennial hemicryptophyte. The plant is winter green dying completely back after flowering in the summer but then producing a small overwintering rosette(s) from a bud(s) on the rootstock. The plant is generally not monocarpic. Reproduction is entirely by seed. Most seeds germinate in the autumn and overwinter as a small rosette although some germinate in the following spring. Newly shed achenes germinate readily, giving rise in nature to seedling populations immediately after the flowering period. Seeds may also germinate after overwintering in the following spring. Flowering is possible after one season providing plants reach an appropriate size. After flowering the plant dies back completely, but in the autumn anover wintering rosette is produced from a bud or buds on the rootstock (Clabby G & Osborne BA. 1999. Mycelis muralis (L.) Dumort.(Lactuca muralis (L.) Gaertner). Journal of ecology, 87:156-172). There is no information about the lifespan of each individual through the new rootstock rosettes. So, the minimum generation time is one year (this can underestimate the actual generation time).

system: Solidago gigantea (giant goldenrod) introduced to Europe from North America
coordinate_notes: coordinates in supp material of the paper. Sample 1 and 2 are the average of several populations
gtime_notes: Solidago gigantea is very simmilar to Solidago altissima (see Solidago altissima GTimeNotes). Solidago gigantea is a tall, erect perennial herb with annual aboveground shoots and persistent belowground rhizomes. Solidago gigantea produces long-creeping plagiotropic, mostly purple or reddish rhizomes, mostly within the upper 10–20 cm of soil. In total, 3–50 rhizomes per ramet emerge close to the base of shoots from the previous year. Higher numbers have been observed after disturbances. Production of seeds, new shoots and new rhizomes occurs every year, and all aboveground shoots die back in autumn. Free carbohydrates are accumulated in the rhizome before the dormant period. Seedlings have never been observed within established patches of S. gigantea, suggesting that seeds are primarily important for long-distance dispersal and the colonization of new sites. However, seedlings may appear after a spring mowing, suggesting that successful establishment is dependent upon open conditions. In most cases, however, population increase is primarily the result of clonal growth. The relative significance of sexual reproduction increases with the age of the clone, whereas clonal growth is most essential during the first years after establishment. Individual clones are often easy to distinguish and frequently achieve 2–5 m diameter. Larger, older clones may contain thousands of ramets. Occasionally clones form ‘fairy circles’ around the initial centre of the genet. Under good conditions, almost all plants reproduce in their first year, and a single ramet produces up to 19,000 achenes. Under resource limited conditions, sexual reproduction is reduced to the benefit of vegetative growth (Weber E & Jakobs G. 2005. Biological flora of central Europe: Solidago gigantea Aiton. Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants, 200:109–118). Generation time should be long but I did not find any estimation. However, Meyer et al 2005 (Meyer G, Clare R, Weber E. 2005. An experimental test of the evolution of increased competitive ability hypothesis in goldenrod, Solidago gigantea. Oecologia, 144:299-307) observed that almost all plants grown from seeds flowered in the secon year, more than a half flowered in the first year. So, in newly colonized areas a generation time of 2 years can be assumed. This would be a far underestimation for established populations.
trait_description: Defence against herbivores, biomass of herbivore insects

Solidago gigantea is a tall, erect perennial herb with annual aboveground shoots and persistent belowground rhizomes. Solidago gigantea produces long-creeping plagiotropic, mostly purple or reddish rhizomes, mostly within the upper 10–20 cm of soil. In total, 3–50 rhizomes per ramet emerge close to the base of shoots from the previous year. Higher numbers have been observed after disturbances. Production of seeds, new shoots and new rhizomes occurs every year, and all aboveground shoots die back in autumn. Free carbohydrates are accumulated in the rhizome before the dormant period. Seedlings have never been observed within established patches of S. gigantea, suggesting that seeds are primarily important for long-distance dispersal and the colonization of new sites. However, seedlings may appear after a spring mowing, suggesting that successful establishment is dependent upon open conditions. In most cases, however, population increase is primarily the result of clonal growth. The relative significance of sexual reproduction increases with the age of the clone, whereas clonal growth is most essential during the first years after establishment. Individual clones are often easy to distinguish and frequently achieve 2–5 m diameter. Larger, older clones may contain thousands of ramets. Occasionally clones form ‘fairy circles’ around the initial centre of the genet. Under good conditions, almost all plants reproduce in their first year, and a single ramet produces up to 19,000 achenes. Under resource limited conditions, sexual reproduction is reduced to the benefit of vegetative growth (Weber E & Jakobs G. 2005. Biological flora of central Europe: Solidago gigantea Aiton. Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants, 200:109–118). Generation time should be long but I did not find any estimation. However, Meyer et al 2005 (Meyer G, Clare R, Weber E. 2005. An experimental test of the evolution of increased competitive ability hypothesis in goldenrod, Solidago gigantea. Oecologia, 144:299-307) observed that almost all plants grown from seeds flowered in the secon year, more than a half flowered in the first year. So, in newly colonized areas a generation time of 2 years can be assumed. This would be a far underestimation for established populations.

Individual clones are often easy to distinguish and frequently achieve 2–5 m diameter. Larger, older clones may contain thousands of ramets. Occasionally clones form ‘fairy circles’ around the initial centre of the genet. Under good conditions, almost all plants reproduce in their first year, and a single ramet produces up to 19,000 achenes. Under resource limited conditions, sexual reproduction is reduced to the benefit of vegetative growth (Weber E & Jakobs G. 2005. Biological flora of central Europe: Solidago gigantea Aiton. Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants, 200:109–118). Generation time should be long but I did not find any estimation. However, Meyer et al 2005 (Meyer G, Clare R, Weber E. 2005. An experimental test of the evolution of increased competitive ability hypothesis in goldenrod, Solidago gigantea. Oecologia, 144:299-307) observed that almost all plants grown from seeds flowered in the secon year, more than a half flowered in the first year. So, in newly colonized areas a generation time of 2 years can be assumed. This would be a far underestimation for established populations.

gtime_notes: “Senecio squalidus is an annual or shortlived perennial plant that normally flowers in its first year of growth (Stace 1997)”. system: Poa annua growing in a new irrigated vs old dry area, at Davis Municipal Golf Course in the Sacramento Valley (California, USA)
coordinate_notes: names of places from paper searched in Google and GoogleMaps. Sample 1 and Sample 2 are sepparated by 50m
gtime_notes: Not in the paper. See Gibeault VA. 1971. Perenniality in Poa annua L. and Law R, Bradshaw AD, Putwain PD. 1977. Life-history variation in Poa annua. Evolution, 31:233-246. There is huge variability in the life history of Poa annua, however, according to Finite rate of increase estimated by Law et al 1977 generation time could be as short as 0.104 years. But, according to Gibeault 1971, seed dormancy varies between 0 and 3 months in different populations and varieties, also winter temperatures below 4.5 ºC preclude germination. So, we estimate a conservative GT of 6 month.
trait_description: prereproductive period (number of days from germination to first flowering)

system: Lolium rigidum developing resistance against glyphosate in Orange, New South Wales, Australia
coordinate_notes: there is no reference to the origin of the population of Sample 1
gtime_notes: Not in the paper but, plants reach maturity at 3-4 month after germination (Chauhan BS, Gill G & Preston C. 2006. Influence of environmental factors on seed germination and seedling emergence of rigid ryegrass (Lolium rigidum). Weed science, 54:1004-1012.) and seeds in the field do not germinate before 6-9 months of seed age (Silsbury JH. 1964. Tiller dynamics, growth, and persistency of Lolium perenne L. and of Lolium rigidum Gaud. Australian Journal of Agricultural Research, 15:9-20.). So a generation time of 1 year seems accurate. 15 years of natural selection plus one generation of selection directed by researchers.

gtime_notes: Rorippa austriaca is a polycarpic, perennial hemicryptophyte. It has the potential to reproduce sexually but was found to spread mainly by vegetative propagation via sprouting from lateral roots. Following plagiotropic growth the lateral roots bend downward and the vertical parts become stark and might eventually develop into tap-roots and produce new shoots and second order lateral roots. In Spring, the species develops flowering stalks. The species flowers copiously in late Spring early Summer. Roroppa austriaca seems to be a rather long-lived species, with fragments of clones attaining ages of at least 13 years (Dietz H, Köhler A & Ullmann I. 2002. Regeneration growth of the invasive clonal forb Rorippa austriaca (Brassicaceae) in relation to fertilization and interspecific competition. Plant Ecology, 158:171-182). Assuming a compensation between mortality and increase in size (and fertility) we estimate a generation time of 6.5 years (possibly an underestimation of the actual generation time).

system: Koeleria macrantha growing with the allelopathic invader Centaurea maculosa at western Montana (USA)
coordinate_notes: coordinates in the paper. Sample 1 and 2 are paired (same location). Coordinates averaged from several populations
gtime_notes: Koeleria macrantha flowers in the first summer after autumn germination and the number of inflorescences at this time is quite low: in cultivation in a good loam this was between 30 and 40, but by the end of 2 years some tussocks had over 200 inflorescences (range 30-291, mean 101.4 ã 13.5). Koeleria macrantha produces a transient seed bank during the summer, when the caryopses are shed, these germinate nearly synchronously in the autumn: there is a complete absence of germinable seeds during spring and early summer (Dixon JM. 2000. Koeleria macrantha (Ledeb.) Schultes (K. alpigena Domin, K. cristata (L.) Pers. pro parte, K. gracilis Pers., K. albescens auct. non DC.). Journal of Ecology, 88:709-726). So the minimum generation time is one year. However, more aged plants produce much more seeds, as we have only information for two years old plants we, comute the genretation time as (1·35+2·101)/(35+101)=1.73. Transition matrices in COMPADRE database are based on tillers (not plants/genets) and include clonal reproduction, so Infinite generation time is estimated.

Koeleria macrantha produces a transient seed bank during the summer, when the caryopses are shed, these germinate nearly synchronously in the autumn: there is a complete absence of germinable seeds during spring and early summer (Dixon JM. 2000. Koeleria macrantha (Ledeb.) Schultes (K. alpigena Domin, K. cristata (L.) Pers. pro parte, K. gracilis Pers., K. albescens auct. non DC.). Journal of Ecology, 88:709-726). So the minimum generation time is one year. However, more aged plants produce much more seeds, as we have only information for two years old plants we, comute the genretation time as (1·35+2·101)/(35+101)=1.73. Transition matrices in COMPADRE database are based on tillers (not plants/genets) and include clonal reproduction, so Infinite generation time is estimated.

system: Lepidium draba introduced to USA in common garden with native Europe populations
comments_on_system: systems in p243, p248, p289 are similar but from different source populations in Europe and North America, partially overlaped
coordinate_notes: Coordinates in supplentary material
gtime_notes: Lepidium draba is a perennial herb, it has a root system that consists of vertical and lateral roots from which new rosettes and flowering shoots arise. Lepidium draba survives and spreads primarily by extremely persistent roots. These roots, with abundant food reserves, overwinter and produce new shootsin the spring (MULLIGAN GA & FINDLAY JN. 1974. The biology of Canadian weeds. 3. Cardaria draba, C. chalepensis, and C. pubescens. Canadian Journal of Plant Science, 54:149-160. Scurfield G. 1962. Cardaria Draba (L.) Desv. The Journal of Ecology, 50:489-499). New plants (grown from seeds) lasted two years to produce flowers (Selleck GW. 1965. An Ecological Study of Lens- and Globe-Podded Hoary Cresses in Saskatchewan. Weeds, 13:1-5). So, the minimum generation time (it underestimates the actuall generation time) is two years. While  most  individuals of Lepidium draba were relatively young (2 to 4 years old), occasional individuals were found to be up to 8 years old (Dietz H & Schweingruber FH. 2002. Annual rings in native and introduced forbs of lower Michigan, USA. Canadian Journal of Botany, 80:642-649). Individuals up to 10 years hold were found (Dietz H. 2002. Plant invasion patches–reconstructing pattern and process by means of herb-chronology. Biological Invasions, 4:211-222). Assuming a compensation between mortality (with age) and increase of fecundity (with age, it still underestimated generation time), the generation time would be 6 years.
trait_description: Generalis herbivore load, core poliphagus herbivores (mean number/site)

gtime_notes: Lepidium draba is a perennial herb, it has a root system that consists of vertical and lateral roots from which new rosettes and flowering shoots arise. Lepidium draba survives and spreads primarily by extremely persistent roots. These roots, with abundant food reserves, overwinter and produce new shootsin the spring (MULLIGAN GA & FINDLAY JN. 1974. The biology of Canadian weeds. 3. Cardaria draba, C. chalepensis, and C. pubescens. Canadian Journal of Plant Science, 54:149-160. Scurfield G. 1962. Cardaria Draba (L.) Desv. The Journal of Ecology, 50:489-499). New plants (grown from seeds) lasted two years to produce flowers (Selleck GW. 1965. An Ecological Study of Lens- and Globe-Podded Hoary Cresses in Saskatchewan. Weeds, 13:1-5). So, the minimum generation time (it underestimates the actuall generation time) is two years. While  most  individuals of Lepidium draba were relatively young (2 to 4 years old), occasional individuals were found to be up to 8 years old (Dietz H & Schweingruber FH. 2002. Annual rings in native and introduced forbs of lower Michigan, USA. Canadian Journal of Botany, 80:642-649). Individuals up to 10 years hold were found (Dietz H. 2002. Plant invasion patches–reconstructing pattern and process by means of herb-chronology. Biological Invasions, 4:211-222). Assuming a compensation between mortality (with age) and increase of fecundity (with age, it still underestimated generation time), the generation time would be 6 years.

system: Jacobaea vulgaris introduced in different countries (USA and New Zealand) from Europe (native range)
coordinate_notes: coordinates in the paper, Sample 1 and 2 average of several populations
gtime_notes: In the paper the authors guess that 100-130 years represents 50 J. vulgaris generations. Jacobaea vulgaris (synonym Senecio jacobaea) is a monocarpic perennial that spends its first year as a rosette. Flowering may take place in the second year, but is often delayed (vernalization depending on a size threshold). Its seeds do not possess innate dormancy. Most of the individuals flowered in the thirth (2 years old) or in fourth (3 years old) year (Van der Meijden E & van der Waals-Kooi RE. 1979. The Population Ecology of Senecio Jacobaea in a Sand Dune System: I. Reproductive Strategy and the Biennial Habit. The Journal of Ecology, 67:131-153). So, generation time is 2.5 years. Generation time computed from transition matrices from COMPADRE database (Matrices 245528, 245531, 245534, 245537, 245540  in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/46711 [18 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0]) are quite variable (from 6.31 to 54.8 years). I kept the GT of 2.5 years, but the uncertainty is large.

Most of the individuals flowered in the thirth (2 years old) or in fourth (3 years old) year (Van der Meijden E & van der Waals-Kooi RE. 1979. The Population Ecology of Senecio Jacobaea in a Sand Dune System: I. Reproductive Strategy and the Biennial Habit. The Journal of Ecology, 67:131-153). So, generation time is 2.5 years. Generation time computed from transition matrices from COMPADRE database (Matrices 245528, 245531, 245534, 245537, 245540  in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/46711 [18 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0]) are quite variable (from 6.31 to 54.8 years). I kept the GT of 2.5 years, but the uncertainty is large.

gtime_notes: Cynoglossum officinale (Boraginaceae) is a monocarpic perennial. None of the plants flowered in their first season, despite their large size, indicating that all plants had a vernalization requirement (WESSELINGH RA, DE JONG TJ, KLINKHAMER PGL, VAN DIJK MJ & SCHLATMANN EGM. 1993. Geographical variation in threshold size for flowering inCynoglossum officinale. Acta Botanica Neerlandica, 42:81–91). Most of the seeds germinate in the first spring following maturation (no seed dormancy). None of the plants flowered in the first year, mortality probability and flowering remain constant after seedling stage, %5 of plants from a cohort flowered in the second year (1 year old) and 7% in the thirth year (2 years old) (De Jong TJ & Klinkhamer PG. 1988. Population ecology of the biennials Cirsium vulgare and Cynoglossum officinale in a coastal sand-dune area. The Journal of Ecology, 76:366-382). Plants may grow vegetatively for 4-5 years before reproducing (de Jong TJ & Klinkhamer PG. 1989. Limiting factors for seed production in Cynoglossum officinale. Oecologia, 80:167-172). Generation matrix was computed from COMPADRE database transition matrix (Matrix 242577 in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). system: Triadica sebifera (Sapium sebiferum) introduced into USA compared with plants from its native range (China)
comments_on_system: systems in p250, p251, p252, p253, p257, p285, p292, p327, p328, p329 are similar but from sligth different source populations in China and North America, partially overlaped.
coordinate_notes: coordinate in the paper, average of several populations
gtime_notes: Generation time computed from the transition matrix in COMPADRE database (Matrix 247906 in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/47232 [06 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0].), based on Renne IJ thesis. Additionally, tree grows rapidly, seedlings are about 1 m tall in the spring of the third year and reace 5 to 8.5 m tall with DBH of 13–17 cm in 10 years, and 10–13 m tall with DBH 30–40 cm in 20 to 30 years. Plants require from 3–8 years to bear, but then contiue to bear for years, averaging 70–100 years (Duke JA. 1983. Handbook of energy crops: Sapium sebiferum(L.) Roxb. Available online at https://hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/duke_energy/Sapium_sebiferum.html Accessed 14 May 2021). Generation time computed from this data and assuming fecundity is directly related to size gives similar generation time (53 ys).
comments: data source within the paper: figure 1

gtime_notes: Life history of C. diffusa range frome annual to short living perenial and a proportion of its seeds have no dormancy. So GT was computed with age at flowering from Thompson & Stout 1991 (Thompson DJ & Stout DG. 1991. Duration of the juvenile period in diffuse knapweed (Centaurea diffusa). Canadian Journal of Botany, 69:368–371). C. diffusa, like other semelparous perennials, flowers after reaching a critical rosette size. The age at which reproduction takes place thus depends on how fast the rosette grow (Powell RD. 1990. The Role of Spatial Pattern in the Population Biology of Centaurea Diffusa. The Journal of Ecology, 78:374-388). C. diffusa reproduces exclusively by seed. Approximately 95% of seedling recruitment takes place during late April (spring) when the ground is moist and temperatures are moderate, the remainder occurs in late September (autum). Spring seedling survival is initially high, but declines rapidly with the onset of the summer drought. The vegetative rosette stage persists for several years before semelparous flowering in dense populations (Powell RD. 1990. The Role of Spatial Pattern in the Population Biology of Centaurea Diffusa. The Journal of Ecology, 78:374-388). C. diffusa requires vernalization (overwinter) to flower (Thompson DJ & Stout DG. 1991. Duration of the juvenile period in diffuse knapweed (Centaurea diffusa). Canadian Journal of Botany, 69:368–371). Each individual plant of C. diffusa can produce seeds with no primary dormancy or different levels of primary dormancy (NOLAN DG & UPADHYAYA MK. 1988. Primary seed dormancy in diffuse and spotted knapweed. Canadian Journal of Plant Science, 68:775-783)

Canadian Journal of Botany, 69:368–371). C. diffusa, like other semelparous perennials, flowers after reaching a critical rosette size. The age at which reproduction takes place thus depends on how fast the rosette grow (Powell RD. 1990. The Role of Spatial Pattern in the Population Biology of Centaurea Diffusa. The Journal of Ecology, 78:374-388). C. diffusa reproduces exclusively by seed. Approximately 95% of seedling recruitment takes place during late April (spring) when the ground is moist and temperatures are moderate, the remainder occurs in late September (autum). Spring seedling survival is initially high, but declines rapidly with the onset of the summer drought. The vegetative rosette stage persists for several years before semelparous flowering in dense populations (Powell RD. 1990. The Role of Spatial Pattern in the Population Biology of Centaurea Diffusa. The Journal of Ecology, 78:374-388). C. diffusa requires vernalization (overwinter) to flower (Thompson DJ & Stout DG. 1991. Duration of the juvenile period in diffuse knapweed (Centaurea diffusa). Primary seed dormancy in diffuse and spotted knapweed. Canadian Journal of Plant Science, 68:775-783)

gtime_notes: Datura stramonium is an annual plant (Núnez‐Farfán J, Cabrales‐Vargas RA & Dirzo R. 1996. Mating system consequences on resistance to herbivory and life history traits in Datura stramonium. American Journal of Botany, 83:1041-1049) and its seeds have primary physical and physiological dormancy (Brown NAC & Bridglall SS. 1987. Preliminary studies of seed dormancy in Datura stramonium. system: Centaurea sulphurea introduced in North America (California, USA) compared with the native populations from Europe (Spain)
coordinate_notes: coordinates in the paper (supp mat). Sample 1 and 2 average of several populations
gtime_notes: All plants flowered and produced seeds in the first year (García Y, Callaway RM, Diaconu A, Montesinos D. 2013. Invasive and non-invasive congeners show similar trait shifts between their same native and non-native ranges. PLoS ONE, 8:e82281). C. sulphurea germinates in the fall and grow vegetatively as rosettes until they bolt in late spring and produce flowering stems. Individual flowers are grouped into heads that are produced for three to four weeks. There is no evidence of seed dormancy (Gerlach Jr JD & Rice KJ. 2003. Testing life history correlates of invasiveness using congeneric plant species. Ecological applications, 13:167-179). So, generation time can be shorter than a year in warm non-stational climates.

system: Oenothera biennis in experimental plots with invertebrate herbivore, at Tompkins County, Ithaca, New York (USA).
coordinate_notes: location name ( Tompkins County, Ithaca, New York) in the paper. Coordinates searched in Google and GoogleMaps. Sample 1 and Sample 2 are from the same sites.
gtime_notes: in the paper: “each year was calculated as 0.72 generations, on the basis of the weighted average of annual and biennial life histories exhibited by plant genotypes in 2007”. However for further genration time of this species: In Oenothera biennis, plants die after flowering (monocarpic). All plants of two years old (3º year of observation) flowered or died. More than 75% (probably more than 85%) of flowering plants are 2 years old (Gross KL. 1981. Predictions of fate from rosette size in four "biennial" plant species: Verbascum thapsus, Oenothera biennis, Daucus carota, and Tragopogon dubius. Oecologia, 48:209–213, Tables 1 and 2). Also, the bigger plants, so the more fecund are the older. Seeds do not show primary dormancy (Baskin CC, Baskin JM. 1994. Germination requirements of Oenothera biennis seeds during burial under natural seasonal temperature cycles. Canadian Journal of Botany, 72:779-782). Most of the seeds germinate in Spring and plants flower also in spring. So generation time is 2-3 years (two of vegetative growing and one year to germination of the new cohort).
comments: data source within the paper: figure 3a

gtime_notes: In Melilotus officinalis, annual individuals overwinter as seeds, biennial individuals overwinter alternatively as seeds and as thick tap root. Natural vegetative reproduction has not been observed. Almost all seedlings appearing in late summer, autumn and early winter die before spring.  Many seedlings appearing in late winter also perish but occasional groups survive and give rise to plants which flower during the same year. Seeds have a long lifespan (40 years) and require scarification to germinate. However, seeds from a similar species (Melilotus albus) is scarified by frozen temperatures and a high proportion of intact seeds germinates in spring after overwintering in the soil (Zhang Y, Zhang K, Ji Y & Tao J. 2020. Physical dormancy and soil seed bank dynamics in seeds of Melilotus albus (Fabaceae). Flora, 266, 151600). So, a 2 years generation time may underestimate the actual generation time but not so far.

system: Rumex crispus introduced in North America (Washignton, USA) compared with the native populations from Europe (Oxfordshire, UK)
coordinate_notes: location in Hulme 2011 Functional Ecology 25:1189-1196
gtime_notes: Rumex crispus is a perennial species. It is able to establish quickly from seed, also has a persistent taproot system, a massive production of seed that remain viable in the seed bank for decades. R. crispus seedlings can emerge throughout the growing season and seeds that remain on the  parent plant over winter posses a certain level of dormancy, leading to later and more intermittent emergence compared to the seeds dispersed in  autumn. Tillage that leads to fragmentation of the root system can stimulate sprouting of new shoots from the regenerative tissue of the taproot. Severed top fragments of roots sprouted faster and produced more shoot biomass than intact rootstocks. Germination of R. crispus seeds is stimulated by light and fluctuating temperatures. Seedling emergence can occur in flushes during the whole vegetation period, depending on weather conditions. Once the juvenile plant is established, the development goes through three phases: the rosette phase, the elongation phase, and the inflorescence phase. Depending on resource availability, R. crispus may flower in its first year or, more commonly, remain in the rosette phase through its first winter. Flowering takes place in late Spring to early Autum, occasional single plants can flower twice in a season. Surviving plants will overwinter as a rosette and can reproduce again in one or several years. Longevity of R. obtusifolius has been reported up to 5 years. Emergence from seeds sown in autumn showed a distinct peak in Spring, while peak emergence for seeds sown in early spring did not occur until late early Summer. Total mortality during the four year period of the field experiment was 24 percent, and total proportion of plants reaching a reproductive stage (i.e. flowered at least once) was 23 percent (Pye A. 2008. Ecological studies of Rumex crispus L. Propagation, competition and demography. Doctoral Thesis, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, Faculty of Natural Resources and Agricultural Sciences, Department of Crop Production Ecology. Upsala). Generation time was computed from demographyc data in Pye 2008, assuming a lifespan of 5 years, a life table was built and generation time was computed.

gtime_notes: Trifolium pratense seedlings appeared from March to May (namely spring cohort) and from September to November (namely autumn cohort) every year. Estimated seedling density ranged yearly from 18 to 1,215 seedlings/m 2 in the spring cohorts and from 1 to 245 seedlings/m 2 in the autumn cohorts, with an average of 199 and 86 seedlings/m2 , respectively. Although the number of flowering individuals decreased yearly, the ratio peaked 2 years after seedling appearance in both kinds of cohorts. (SAKANOUE S. 2002. system: Tussilago farfara introduced in North America (Washignton, USA) compared with the native populations from Europe (Oxfordshire, UK)
coordinate_notes: location in Hulme 2011 Functional Ecology 25:1189-1196
gtime_notes: Tussilago farfara is a rhizomatous perennial. Germination takes place shortly after the seeds are shed in April or May (spring), and in suitable habitats a tap root is quickly developed. During the first summer contractile adventitious roots develop on the lowest nodes of the stem, followed shortly by rhizomes, initiated in the same region. By the autumn several large leaves may be present, rhizomes well developed, and inflorescence ('flower') buds will usually have been formed. In favourable situations vegetative reproduction occurs in the first season, the tips of certain rhizomes growing upwards to produce new plants. During the winter the leaves die, and all that is usually visible at the soil surface is a cluster of flower buds on the 'stock'. The stock is the non-rhizomatous portion of the stem, which bears the leaves in summer and the flowers in the following spring: it is normally short and thick, with very close internodes (Raunkiaer 1934). The flower buds continue their development during the winter, and early in the following spring the peduncles elongate rapidly and the flowers open. Seed dispersal occurs in April and May (spring). During the flowering period leaves are expanded by the new vegetative shoots at the tips of those rhizomes which were formed in the previous year. The flowering stock and the peduncles normally die after the seeds are shed, leading to fragmentation of the rhizome system. The new vegetative plants follow the same cycle of development as those in the previous year. It follows that normally rhizomes initiated in one year produce leafy shoots in the second year, and these shoots produce flowers in the third year (2 years old) of life of the rhizomes. After this they usually die, leaving further growth to new rhizome (Ogden J. 1974. The Reproductive Strategy of Higher Plants: II. The Reproductive Strategy of Tussilago Farfara L. The Journal of Ecology, 62:291-324). Generation Time is considered as the number of years required for a species to start producing seeds (this can underestimate the actual generation time) according to: Engler R, Randin CF, Vittoz P, Czáka T, Beniston M, Zimmermann NE & Guisan A. 2009. Predicting future distributions of mountain plants under climate change: does dispersal capacity matter?. Ecography, 32:34-45.

gtime_notes: Cichorium intybus L. is a biennial plant. In order to be florally induced, chicory must undergo an exposure to low temperature (3 weeks at 4 °C) that can be applied to germinating seeds or to the entire plant. Cichorium intybus seeds do not show any dormancy (Corbineau F & Come D. 1990. Germinability and quality of Cichorium intybus L. seeds. In VI Symposium on the Timing of Field Production of Vegetables 267:183-190). So, generation time is one year.

coordinate_notes: location names in the paper. Coordinates searched in Google Maps
gtime_notes: In Melilotus officinalis, annual individuals overwinter as seeds, biennial individuals overwinter alternatively as seeds and as thick tap root. Natural vegetative reproduction has not been observed. Almost all seedlings appearing in late summer, autumn and early winter die before spring.  Many seedlings appearing in late winter also perish but occasional groups survive and give rise to plants which flower during the same year. In contrast, seedlings appearing in Spring have the best chance of survival but invariably are biennial. (Turkington RA, Cavers PB, Empel E. 1978. The biology of Canadian weeds. 29. Melilotus alba Desr. and M. officinalis (L.) Lam. Can J Plant Sci, 58:523–537). Plants always die after flowering (monocarpic). Seeds have a long lifespan (40 years) and require scarification to germinate. However, seeds from a similar species (Melilotus albus) is scarified by frozen temperatures and a high proportion of intact seeds germinates in spring after overwintering in the soil (Zhang Y, Zhang K, Ji Y & Tao J. 2020. Physical dormancy and soil seed bank dynamics in seeds of Melilotus albus (Fabaceae). Flora, 266, 151600). So, a 2 years generation time may underestimate the actual generation time but not so far.

gtime_notes: Plantago lanceolata (ribwort plantain) is a short-lived perennial species with a basal rosette. It germinates in the fall and spring and flowers in mid summer. It remains green all year. Only 7% of the population remained alive after 4.5yr. Individuals in the field flowered for the first  time in Spring of year 2 (one year old). system: Rumex crispus introduced in North America (Washignton, USA) compared with the native populations from Europe (Oxfordshire, UK)
coordinate_notes: location names in the paper. Coordinates searched in Google Maps
gtime_notes: Rumex crispus is a perennial species. It is able to establish quickly from seed, also has a persistent taproot system, a massive production of seed that remain viable in the seed bank for decades. R. crispus seedlings can emerge throughout the growing season and seeds that remain on the  parent plant over winter posses a certain level of dormancy, leading to later and more intermittent emergence compared to the seeds dispersed in  autumn. Tillage that leads to fragmentation of the root system can stimulate sprouting of new shoots from the regenerative tissue of the taproot. Severed top fragments of roots sprouted faster and produced more shoot biomass than intact rootstocks. Germination of R. crispus seeds is stimulated by light and fluctuating temperatures. Seedling emergence can occur in flushes during the whole vegetation period, depending on weather conditions. Once the juvenile plant is established, the development goes through three phases: the rosette phase, the elongation phase, and the inflorescence phase. Depending on resource availability, R. crispus may flower in its first year or, more commonly, remain in the rosette phase through its first winter. Flowering takes place in late Spring to early Autum, occasional single plants can flower twice in a season. Surviving plants will overwinter as a rosette and can reproduce again in one or several years. Longevity of R. obtusifolius has been reported up to 5 years. Emergence from seeds sown in autumn showed a distinct peak in Spring, while peak emergence for seeds sown in early spring did not occur until late early Summer. Total mortality during the four year period of the field experiment was 24 percent, and total proportion of plants reaching a reproductive stage (i.e. flowered at least once) was 23 percent (Pye A. 2008. Ecological studies of Rumex crispus L. Propagation, competition and demography. Doctoral Thesis, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, Faculty of Natural Resources and Agricultural Sciences, Department of Crop Production Ecology. Upsala). Generation time was computed from demographyc data in Pye 2008, assuming a lifespan of 5 years, a life table was built and generation time was computed.

system: Trifolium pratense introduced in North America (Washignton, USA) compared with the native populations from Europe (Oxfordshire, UK)
coordinate_notes: location names in the paper. Coordinates searched in Google Maps
gtime_notes: Trifolium pratense seedlings appeared from March to May (namely spring cohort) and from September to November (namely autumn cohort) every year. Estimated seedling density ranged yearly from 18 to 1,215 seedlings/m 2 in the spring cohorts and from 1 to 245 seedlings/m 2 in the autumn cohorts, with an average of 199 and 86 seedlings/m2 , respectively. Half-life ranged yearly from 4 to 63 days for the spring cohorts and from 33 to 248 days for the autumn cohorts, with an average of 42 and 135 days, respectively. Of the 13,485 seedlings marked, no individuals survived for more than 4 years. Most of the individuals undergoing flowering (hereafter referred to as “flowering individuals”) originated from the autumn cohorts. Thirty-two percent of the survivors began to flower in the first summer after their appearance. Ratio of flowering individuals to survivors rose to 81% in the second summer and fell to 50% in the third summer. Although the number of flowering individuals decreased yearly, the ratio peaked 2 years after seedling appearance in both kinds of cohorts. (SAKANOUE S. 2002. Seedling appearance, survival andflowering of Trifolium pratense in a cutting meadow. Japan Agricultural Research Quarterly, 36:235–241). Table of life and generation time were computed based on demographyc information from this paper.

system: Tussilago farfara introduced in North America (Washignton, USA) compared with the native populations from Europe (Oxfordshire, UK)
coordinate_notes: location names in the paper. Coordinates searched in Google Maps
gtime_notes: Tussilago farfara is a rhizomatous perennial. Germination takes place shortly after the seeds are shed in April or May (spring), and in suitable habitats a tap root is quickly developed. During the first summer contractile adventitious roots develop on the lowest nodes of the stem, followed shortly by rhizomes, initiated in the same region. By the autumn several large leaves may be present, rhizomes well developed, and inflorescence ('flower') buds will usually have been formed. In favourable situations vegetative reproduction occurs in the first season, the tips of certain rhizomes growing upwards to produce new plants. During the winter the leaves die, and all that is usually visible at the soil surface is a cluster of flower buds on the 'stock'. The stock is the non-rhizomatous portion of the stem, which bears the leaves in summer and the flowers in the following spring: it is normally short and thick, with very close internodes (Raunkiaer 1934). The flower buds continue their development during the winter, and early in the following spring the peduncles elongate rapidly and the flowers open. Seed dispersal occurs in April and May (spring). During the flowering period leaves are expanded by the new vegetative shoots at the tips of those rhizomes which were formed in the previous year. The flowering stock and the peduncles normally die after the seeds are shed, leading to fragmentation of the rhizome system. The new vegetative plants follow the same cycle of development as those in the previous year. It follows that normally rhizomes initiated in one year produce leafy shoots in the second year, and these shoots produce flowers in the third year (2 years old) of life of the rhizomes. After this they usually die, leaving further growth to new rhizome (Ogden J. 1974. The Reproductive Strategy of Higher Plants: II. The Reproductive Strategy of Tussilago Farfara L. The Journal of Ecology, 62:291-324). Generation Time is considered as the number of years required for a species to start producing seeds (this can underestimate the actual generation time) according to: Engler R, Randin CF, Vittoz P, Czáka T, Beniston M, Zimmermann NE & Guisan A. 2009. Predicting future distributions of mountain plants under climate change: does dispersal capacity matter?. Ecography, 32:34-45.

system: Solidago altissima plants in plots in where above-ground herbivores was manipulated, at Whipple Farm, Tompkins Co., NY, USA
coordinate_notes: coordinates in Carson, W. P., & Root, R. B. (2000). Herbivory and plant species coexistence: community regulation by an outbreaking phytophagous insect. Ecological monographs, 70(1), 73-99. Sample 1 and 2 are few meters apart each other.
gtime_notes: Solidago altissima, is a perennial. Most ramets emerge in Spring from the apical tips of underground rhizomes, and increase in height until mid Summer, at which time flower heads begin to form. The apical tips of some rhizomes emerge the previous season, but the leaves of such rhizomes do not expand until spring (i.e. there are no overwintering rosettes). Rhizome growth is sympodial. The above-ground portion of ramets die over winter, and their daughter rhizomes remain dormant until the following spring. Ramets are not produced at the same node in successive years, so genet survival depends upon the new ramets that emerge in the spring from overwintering rhizomes. Although above-ground shoots die after one season, roots and rhizome connections persist for up to 5-6 years (fragmentation, not death) (Cain ML. 1990. Models of Clonal Growth in Solidago Altissima. The Journal of Ecology, 78:27-46). Clones of S. canadensis increase in both size and density and can persist for a considerable number of years, estimated at more than 100 yr (Werner, P. A., GROSS, R. S., & BRADBURY, I. K. (1980). THE BIOLOGY OF CANADIAN WEEDS.: 45. Solidago canadensis L. Canadian Journal of Plant Science, 60:1393-1409). Germination within the established vegetation was very rare: only 12 out of 150000 experimentally sown seeds (0.008%) became seedlings. The survival and growth of seedlings transplanted into closed vegetation increased with age and developmental stage. Nevertheless, no transplants flowered during the 24 months over which their fate was followed (Meyer AH & Schmid B. 1999. Seed dynamics and seedling establishment in the invading perennial Solidago altissima under different experimental treatments. Journal of Ecology, 87:28-41). So, it seems the generation time in Solidago altissima should be very long but we did not find any approximation. COMPADRE database transition matrix (Matrix 245611 in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/46727 [21 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0]) leads to a generation time of 6723 years.

The maximum lifespan for tetraploid individuals is 9 years (Boggs KW & Story JM. 1987. The population age structure of spotted knapweed (Centaurea maculosa) in Montana. Weed Science, 35:194-198).
