system: Solidago gigantea (giant goldenrod) introduced to Europe from North America
coordinate_notes: coordinates in Meyer, G., Clare, R., & Weber, E. (2005). An experimental test of the evolution of increased competitive ability hypothesis in goldenrod, Solidago gigantea. Oecologia, 144(2), 299-307. Sample 1 and 2 are the average of several populations
gtime_notes: Solidago gigantea is very simmilar to Solidago altissima (see Solidago altissima GTimeNotes). Solidago gigantea is a tall, erect perennial herb with annual aboveground shoots and persistent belowground rhizomes. Solidago gigantea produces long-creeping plagiotropic, mostly purple or reddish rhizomes, mostly within the upper 10–20 cm of soil. In total, 3–50 rhizomes per ramet emerge close to the base of shoots from the previous year. Higher numbers have been observed after disturbances. Production of seeds, new shoots and new rhizomes occurs every year, and all aboveground shoots die back in autumn. Free carbohydrates are accumulated in the rhizome before the dormant period. Seedlings have never been observed within established patches of S. gigantea, suggesting that seeds are primarily important for long-distance dispersal and the colonization of new sites. However, seedlings may appear after a spring mowing, suggesting that successful establishment is dependent upon open conditions. In most cases, however, population increase is primarily the result of clonal growth. The relative significance of sexual reproduction increases with the age of the clone, whereas clonal growth is most essential during the first years after establishment. Individual clones are often easy to distinguish and frequently achieve 2–5 m diameter. Larger, older clones may contain thousands of ramets. Occasionally clones form ‘fairy circles’ around the initial centre of the genet. Under good conditions, almost all plants reproduce in their first year, and a single ramet produces up to 19,000 achenes. Under resource limited conditions, sexual reproduction is reduced to the benefit of vegetative growth (Weber E & Jakobs G. 2005. Biological flora of central Europe: Solidago gigantea Aiton. Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants, 200:109–118). Generation time should be long but I did not find any estimation. However, Meyer et al 2005 (Meyer G, Clare R, Weber E. 2005. An experimental test of the evolution of increased competitive ability hypothesis in goldenrod, Solidago gigantea. Oecologia, 144:299-307) observed that almost all plants grown from seeds flowered in the secon year, more than a half flowered in the first year. So, in newly colonized areas a generation time of 2 years can be assumed. This would be a far underestimation for established populations.

Solidago gigantea is a tall, erect perennial herb with annual aboveground shoots and persistent belowground rhizomes. Solidago gigantea produces long-creeping plagiotropic, mostly purple or reddish rhizomes, mostly within the upper 10–20 cm of soil. In total, 3–50 rhizomes per ramet emerge close to the base of shoots from the previous year. Higher numbers have been observed after disturbances. Production of seeds, new shoots and new rhizomes occurs every year, and all aboveground shoots die back in autumn. Free carbohydrates are accumulated in the rhizome before the dormant period. Seedlings have never been observed within established patches of S. gigantea, suggesting that seeds are primarily important for long-distance dispersal and the colonization of new sites. However, seedlings may appear after a spring mowing, suggesting that successful establishment is dependent upon open conditions. In most cases, however, population increase is primarily the result of clonal growth. The relative significance of sexual reproduction increases with the age of the clone, whereas clonal growth is most essential during the first years after establishment. Individual clones are often easy to distinguish and frequently achieve 2–5 m diameter. Larger, older clones may contain thousands of ramets. Occasionally clones form ‘fairy circles’ around the initial centre of the genet. Under good conditions, almost all plants reproduce in their first year, and a single ramet produces up to 19,000 achenes. Under resource limited conditions, sexual reproduction is reduced to the benefit of vegetative growth (Weber E & Jakobs G. 2005. Biological flora of central Europe: Solidago gigantea Aiton. Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants, 200:109–118). Generation time should be long but I did not find any estimation. However, Meyer et al 2005 (Meyer G, Clare R, Weber E. 2005. An experimental test of the evolution of increased competitive ability hypothesis in goldenrod, Solidago gigantea. Oecologia, 144:299-307) observed that almost all plants grown from seeds flowered in the secon year, more than a half flowered in the first year. So, in newly colonized areas a generation time of 2 years can be assumed. This would be a far underestimation for established populations.

gtime_notes: Jacobaea vulgaris (synonym Senecio jacobaea) is a monocarpic perennial that spends its first year as a rosette. Flowering may take place in the second year, but is often delayed (vernalization depending on a size threshold). Its seeds do not possess innate dormancy. Most of the individuals flowered in the thirth (2 years old) or in fourth (3 years old) year (Van der Meijden E & van der Waals-Kooi RE. 1979. The Population Ecology of Senecio Jacobaea in a Sand Dune System: I. Reproductive Strategy and the Biennial Habit. The Journal of Ecology, 67:131-153). So, generation time is 2.5 years. Generation time computed from transition matrices from COMPADRE database (Matrices 245528, 245531, 245534, 245537, 245540  in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/46711 [18 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0]) are quite variable (from 6.31 to 54.8 years). I kept the GT of 2.5 years, but the uncertainty is large.

coordinate_notes: coordinates in the paper. Sample 1 and 2 are the average of several populations
gtime_notes: Lepidium draba is a perennial herb, it has a root system that consists of vertical and lateral roots from which new rosettes and flowering shoots arise. Lepidium draba survives and spreads primarily by extremely persistent roots. These roots, with abundant food reserves, overwinter and produce new shootsin the spring (MULLIGAN GA & FINDLAY JN. 1974. The biology of Canadian weeds. 3. Cardaria draba, C. chalepensis, and C. pubescens. Canadian Journal of Plant Science, 54:149-160. Scurfield G. 1962. Cardaria Draba (L.) Desv. The Journal of Ecology, 50:489-499). New plants (grown from seeds) lasted two years to produce flowers (Selleck GW. 1965. An Ecological Study of Lens- and Globe-Podded Hoary Cresses in Saskatchewan. Weeds, 13:1-5). So, the minimum generation time (it underestimates the actuall generation time) is two years. While  most  individuals of Lepidium draba were relatively young (2 to 4 years old), occasional individuals were found to be up to 8 years old (Dietz H & Schweingruber FH. 2002. Annual rings in native and introduced forbs of lower Michigan, USA. Canadian Journal of Botany, 80:642-649). Individuals up to 10 years hold were found (Dietz H. 2002. Plant invasion patches–reconstructing pattern and process by means of herb-chronology. Biological Invasions, 4:211-222). Assuming a compensation between mortality (with age) and increase of fecundity (with age, it still underestimated generation time), the generation time would be 6 years.

system: Lythrum salicaria (purple loosestrife) introduced into North America diverged from native European plants
comments_on_system: Systems in p012, p291, p306, p315, p316 are similar. Same situation with different source populations

gtime_notes: "The species has been described as a facultative annual because it can set seed in one growing season (Shipley and Parent 1991, Johansson and Keddy 1991), however, this description is misleading because the species is not semelparous. sample1: Solidago altissima population with 3-4 years of Corythucha marmorata herbivory
sample2: Solidago altissima population with 11-12 years of Corythucha marmorata herbivory
coordinate_notes: coordinates in supp material of the paper
gtime_notes: Solidago altissima, is a perennial. Most ramets emerge in Spring from the apical tips of underground rhizomes, and increase in height until mid Summer, at which time flower heads begin to form. The apical tips of some rhizomes emerge the previous season, but the leaves of such rhizomes do not expand until spring (i.e. there are no overwintering rosettes). Rhizome growth is sympodial. The above-ground portion of ramets die over winter, and their daughter rhizomes remain dormant until the following spring. Ramets are not produced at the same node in successive years, so genet survival depends upon the new ramets that emerge in the spring from overwintering rhizomes. Although above-ground shoots die after one season, roots and rhizome connections persist for up to 5-6 years (fragmentation, not death) (Cain ML. 1990. Models of Clonal Growth in Solidago Altissima. The Journal of Ecology, 78:27-46). Clones of S. canadensis increase in both size and density and can persist for a considerable number of years, estimated at more than 100 yr (Werner, P. A., GROSS, R. S., & BRADBURY, I. K. (1980). THE BIOLOGY OF CANADIAN WEEDS.: 45. Solidago canadensis L. Canadian Journal of Plant Science, 60:1393-1409). Germination within the established vegetation was very rare: only 12 out of 150000 experimentally sown seeds (0.008%) became seedlings. The survival and growth of seedlings transplanted into closed vegetation increased with age and developmental stage. Nevertheless, no transplants flowered during the 24 months over which their fate was followed (Meyer AH & Schmid B. 1999. Seed dynamics and seedling establishment in the invading perennial Solidago altissima under different experimental treatments. Journal of Ecology, 87:28-41). So, it seems the generation time in Solidago altissima should be very long but we did not find any approximation. COMPADRE database transition matrix (Matrix 245611 in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/46727 [21 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0]) leads to a generation time of 6723 years.

The apical tips of some rhizomes emerge the previous season, but the leaves of such rhizomes do not expand until spring (i.e. there are no overwintering rosettes). Rhizome growth is sympodial. The above-ground portion of ramets die over winter, and their daughter rhizomes remain dormant until the following spring. Ramets are not produced at the same node in successive years, so genet survival depends upon the new ramets that emerge in the spring from overwintering rhizomes. Although above-ground shoots die after one season, roots and rhizome connections persist for up to 5-6 years (fragmentation, not death) (Cain ML. 1990. Models of Clonal Growth in Solidago Altissima. The Journal of Ecology, 78:27-46). Clones of S. canadensis increase in both size and density and can persist for a considerable number of years, estimated at more than 100 yr (Werner, P. A., GROSS, R. S., & BRADBURY, I. K. (1980). THE BIOLOGY OF CANADIAN WEEDS.: 45. Solidago canadensis L. Canadian Journal of Plant Science, 60:1393-1409). Germination within the established vegetation was very rare: only 12 out of 150000 experimentally sown seeds (0.008%) became seedlings. The survival and growth of seedlings transplanted into closed vegetation increased with age and developmental stage. Nevertheless, no transplants flowered during the 24 months over which their fate was followed (Meyer AH & Schmid B. 1999. Seed dynamics and seedling establishment in the invading perennial Solidago altissima under different experimental treatments. Journal of Ecology, 87:28-41). So, it seems the generation time in Solidago altissima should be very long but we did not find any approximation. COMPADRE database transition matrix (Matrix 245611 in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/46727 [21 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0]) leads to a generation time of 6723 years.

gtime_notes: Rumex acetosa is a polycarpic perennial which possesses a limited capacity for vegetative propagation (Voesenek LACJ & Blom CWPM. 1992. Germination and emergence ofRumexin river flood-plains. I. Timing of germination and seedbank characteristics. Acta Botanica Neerlandica, 41: 319–329). The mature plant overwinters as a basal rosette and produces one or more inflorescences in spring. The inflorescences elongate at the beginning of April and bloom through April and May. The seeds mature from late April onward, just after flowering. Therefore, flowering and seeding overlap within individual inflorescence stems and branches (Matsuhisa S & Ushimaru A. 2019. Does sexual dimorphism exist in flowering phenology traits in anemophilous dioecious species? A test with Rumex acetosa. American journal of botany, 106: 1356-1364). No dormancy was observed in Rumex acetosa, and seeds survive in optimal conditions at least 3 years (Steinbauer GP & Grigsby B. 1960. Dormancy and germination of the docks (Rumex spp.). Proceedings of the Association of Official Seed Analysts, 50: 112-117). A generation time of 2 years can underestimate the actual generation time.

gtime_notes: All plants flowered and produced seeds in the first year (García Y, Callaway RM, Diaconu A, Montesinos D. 2013. Invasive and non-invasive congeners show similar trait shifts between their same native and non-native ranges. PLoS ONE, 8:e82281). Plants germinate in Autumn, stay as a rosette in winter and flowered late in summer (Thomsen CD. 1996. Yellow starthistle biology and control Vol. 21541 UCANR Publications). Centaurea solstitialis requires about 2140 degree days (over 2 ºC) for 50% of the plants to reach seed dispersal, It does not require vernalization to flower (Roche CT, Thill DC & Shafii B. 1997. Reproductive phenology in yellow starthistle (Centaurea solstitialis). Weed Science, 45:763-770). Seeds do not show primary (innate) dormancy, but secondary induced (Joley DB, Maddox DM, Schoenig SE & Mackey BE. 2003. Parameters affecting germinability and seed bank dynamics in dimorphic achenes of Centaurea solstitialis in California. Canadian Journal of Botany, 81:993-1007). So, generation time can be shorter than a year in warm non-stational climates.

gtime_notes: Ambrosia artemisiifolia is a wind-pollinated, monoecious annual herb, which germinates in the spring and sets fruit in the autumn. Ambrosia artemisiifolia is sensitive to freezing. Late spring frosts kill seedlings and the first autumn frosts terminate the growing season. Ambrosia artemisiifolia forms a persistent soil seed bank as aresult of complex germination strategies. Seeds are dormant following their dispersal in autumn. This primary (innate) dormancy is then broken by low winter temperatures (optimallya few days around 4°C) and seeds that donot germinate the next spring enter secondary (induced) dormancy (Essl F, Biró K, Brandes D, Broennimann O, Bullock JM, Chapman DS, ... & Follak S. 2015. system: Jacobaea vulgaris (formerly Senecio jacobaea) was introduced in New Zealand from Europe, comparison between population origins in a common garden experiment
comments_on_system: related to s1708 and s1764
coordinate_notes: coordinates in the paper
gtime_notes: Jacobaea vulgaris (synonym Senecio jacobaea) is a monocarpic perennial that spends its first year as a rosette. Flowering may take place in the second year, but is often delayed (vernalization depending on a size threshold). Its seeds do not possess innate dormancy. Most of the individuals flowered in the thirth (2 years old) or in fourth (3 years old) year (Van der Meijden E & van der Waals-Kooi RE. 1979. The Population Ecology of Senecio Jacobaea in a Sand Dune System: I. Reproductive Strategy and the Biennial Habit. The Journal of Ecology, 67:131-153). So, generation time is 2.5 years. Generation time computed from transition matrices from COMPADRE database (Matrices 245528, 245531, 245534, 245537, 245540  in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/46711 [18 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0]) are quite variable (from 6.31 to 54.8 years). I kept the GT of 2.5 years, but the uncertainty is large.
comments: data source within the paper: figure 2a

sample2: North American seeds in Hawaii experiment
coordinate_notes: location names in the paper Siemann 2001, Ecology Letters 4: 514-518. Coordinates searched in Google maps. Sample 2 is from Texas (with no more specifications). I assume the same origin than in paper Rogers & Siemann 2005, Plant Ecology 181:57-68
gtime_notes: Generation time computed from the transition matrix in COMPADRE database (Matrix 247906 in COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database (2021). Available from: https://www.compadre-db.org/Species/47232 [06 May 2021, Version 6.21.1.0].), based on Renne IJ thesis. Additionally, tree grows rapidly, seedlings are about 1 m tall in the spring of the third year and reace 5 to 8.5 m tall with DBH of 13–17 cm in 10 years, and 10–13 m tall with DBH 30–40 cm in 20 to 30 years. Plants require from 3–8 years to bear, but then contiue to bear for years, averaging 70–100 years (Duke JA. 1983. Handbook of energy crops: Sapium sebiferum(L.) Roxb. Available online at https://hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/duke_energy/Sapium_sebiferum.html Accessed 14 May 2021). Generation time computed from this data and assuming fecundity is directly related to size gives similar generation time (53 ys).
